public_rationale: The evidence supports persistence of a generalization weakness: arithmetic performance still deteriorated as inputs grew less familiar. Successful addition transfer shows that abstract rule learning was not wholly out of reach. The supported reading is therefore a recurring limitation, not an unchanged universal inability or proof of the same internal mechanism as in the early 1990s.
limitations: The conclusion depends on the ordinary reading of a persistent weakness.
The categorical reading that neural networks cannot learn abstract rules is not supported.
The historical analogy is assessed behaviorally, not as a causal claim.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: The weakness of neural networks in learning abstract, similarity-independent rules, identified in the early 1990s, still persists in current deep learning.

statement.excerpt: Thirty years later, the same Achilles’ Heel remains.
statement.document_title: “Math is hard” — if you are an LLM – and why that matters

our_interpretation: The plain reading is that learning rules which transfer beyond familiar training examples remained a weakness of contemporary deep learning.
Persistence of a weakness does not require every neural architecture to fail every rule-learning task.
The historical comparison concerns the type of behavioral limitation. It does not establish identical internal mechanisms across three decades.
The target is the 2023 research state through publication. With no regular reporting period, I use the current calendar year through 2023-10-19.
criteria.support_condition: Contemporary controlled studies document continuing failures to transfer learned rules to unfamiliar problem sizes or structures despite strong performance on familiar cases.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Contemporary studies establish broadly dependable rule transfer across unfamiliar sizes and structures, showing that the described generalization weakness had been overcome. Individual successes qualify the claim but do not alone establish this.

evidence.excerpt: handling larger digit ranges poses a greater challenge
evidence.locator: Section 4.1.4, Generalization Analysis, discussion of Table 7
evidence.explanation: Accuracy declined as digit ranges increased, even after additional training on longer examples. This supports a continuing reliability weakness, although mixed arithmetic operations and exposure to longer examples prevent treating it as a clean test of wholly unseen lengths.

Models trained on five-digit addition achieved 99.9% accuracy on ten-digit inputs and 98.3% on fifteen-digit inputs, demonstrating substantial transfer beyond training lengths. Accuracy fell to 21.3% at twenty digits, so the success qualifies an absolute inability claim while remaining compatible with a persistent weakness.
